title: Characterization and Active Control of Position-Dependent Timing Dynamics in Superconducting Strip Detectors
authors: Sahil R. Patel, Kristen M. Parzuchowski, Eli Mueller, Boris Korzh, Emanuel Knehr, Adam N. McCaughan, Martin J. Stevens, Matthew D. Shaw, Jason P. Allmaras
abstract: Superconducting strip single-photon detectors (SSPDs) have emerged as scalable, wide-strip variants of traditional nanowire counterparts. Despite practical advantages including improved optical fill factors and enhanced signal-to-noise ratios the fundamental detection physics governing these micro-scale geometries remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the underlying photoresponse of a 20 um-wide tungsten silicide SSPD, demonstrating a slew-rate-corrected timing jitter of 13.2 ps at 532 nm and 20.5 ps at 1550 nm, alongside saturated internal detection efficiency up to 1550 nm. Using focused free-space optical scanning, we reveal that detector timing jitter is strongly influenced by a spatially dependent slew rate between edge and center absorption events. To mitigate this impact, we utilize a parallel superconducting rail architecture to actively redistribute supercurrent. This in-situ tuning minimizes the latency mismatch and mitigates thermally activated intrinsic dark counts, extending the device's ability to operate at higher temperatures. Finally, comparing these dynamics with time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) modeling elucidates the physical origins of the position-dependent photoresponse, highlighting how superconducting rails or specialized readout electronics can mitigate negative impacts on timing jitter.
summary: This research characterizes the timing jitter in Superconducting Strip Detectors (SSPDs), finding that the detection timing is highly dependent on where the photon is absorbed across the strip width. By implementing an active control system using parallel superconducting rails, the authors successfully minimize this position-dependent timing mismatch, improving the detector's overall temporal resolution.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental physics governing Superconducting Strip Detectors (SSPDs), specifically addressing the issue of position-dependent timing jitter caused by spatially varying superconducting slew rates.
main_result: Active control using parallel superconducting rails can successfully mitigate the latency mismatch caused by transverse variations in the slew rate, leading to reduced and more uniform timing jitter across the detector width.
method: The study combines experimental characterization using focused optical scanning and jitter histogram analysis with theoretical modeling using Time-Dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) equations.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting strip detector (SSPD) made of tungsten silicide, whose detection dynamics are modeled using TDGL theory to capture the superconducting-to-normal state transition.
key_observables: Slew-rate-corrected timing jitter (at 532 nm and 1550 nm), internal detection efficiency, and the shape of the jitter histogram (bimodal vs. Gaussian).
important_parameters: Detector width ($20 \mu	ext{m}$), operating wavelengths (532 nm, 1550 nm), and the applied current in the superconducting control rails.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the transverse variation in the slew rate is the dominant source of timing jitter, and that applying a counter-current via superconducting rails can effectively equalize the detection latency.
figures_summary: Figures show the location-dependent slew rate map, the emergence of bimodal jitter histograms based on the trigger threshold, and the suppression of this bimodality using superconducting rails, alongside simulated voltage transients comparing edge vs. center detection.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first characterizing the position-dependent photoresponse and jitter of the SSPD. It then introduces the active control mechanism using superconducting rails to counteract the observed spatial variations, validating the mitigation effect through both measurement and TDGL simulation.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete example of using superconducting circuit physics (supercurrent redistribution) to actively manage timing jitter in a detector, which has implications for high-precision quantum measurements and quantum communication.

Fig. 5 Elevated-temperature operation enabled by active current redistribution. (a) Subtracted photoresponse count rate (PCR) and dark count rate (DCR) at 1.0 K under 1064 nm illumination. The detector demonstrates a distinct plateau across varying active rail currents. (b) Detector response at an elevated temperature of 1.625 K. Without active current redistribution (0 mA rail current), thermally activated vortex entry increases intrinsic DCR sharply, collapsing the plateau. Applying a rail current (up to 14.5 mA) mitigates edge-crowding and systematically shifts the DCR onset, successfully recovering a viable operational plateau.
